Evaluating a crystal ball - part 1

The future is now

Session 18: Evaluating classification models for cognitive impairment prediction.

Key dataset: ad_validation_logistic with observed classes and predicted probabilities.

The ABCD Framework

A useful way to remember prediction-model evaluation:

  • A = Calibration-in-the-large
  • B = Calibration slope
  • C = C-statistic / Discrimination
  • D = Decision curve / Clinical usefulness

This framework separates statistical performance from clinical usefulness.

Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4155437/

Case Study: Cognitive Impairment Prediction

We evaluate a logistic regression model predicting cognitive impairment from:

  • Age
  • Sex (male)
  • Tau protein
  • Phosphorylated tau
  • Amyloid beta 42
  • APOE genotype

Outcome: Impaired vs Control (gold-standard neurophyschological test)

The Prediction Model

The model was trained on a separate training set:

\[ impairment_i \sim age + male + tau + p\_tau + Ab\_42 + genotype \]

where predictors are measured in cerebrospinal fluid via lumbar puncture.

Tau and p_tau: biomarkers related to neurofibrillary tangles Ab_42: Amyloid beta 42 forms plaques in Alzheimer’s disease Genotype: APOE allele pairs (E2E2, E2E3, E3E3, E3E4, E2E4, E4E4)

Dataset Visualization

Tau vs p-tau by genotype and diagnosis

Evaluating Prediction Models

What We Need

A prediction model can be evaluated from two things:

  • What actually happened (observed outcome)
  • What the model predicted (predicted probabilities)

Here we use predictions from a pre-trained logistic regression model.

We work with ad_validation_logistic which contains: - Class: the observed outcome - .pred_impaired: predicted probability of impairment

No need to fit a model; we simply evaluate its predictions.

The Validation Data

Class = observed outcome. .pred_impaired = predicted probability of impairment.

   .pred_impaired .pred_control    Class
1      0.40306887     0.5969311  control
3      0.66547506     0.3345249  control
5      0.71154002     0.2884600  control
7      0.29307658     0.7069234  control
9      0.01425278     0.9857472  control
11     0.56453589     0.4354641 impaired

The dataset contains 167 observations with: - Class: factor with levels “control” and “impaired” - .pred_impaired: numeric predicted probabilities

Confusion Matrix

How many were correctly classified?

          Truth
Prediction impaired control
  impaired       25      14
  control        19     109

Pattern observed: - Many more control participants (123) than cognitively impaired (44) - Only 25/44 impaired were labeled correctly (56.8%) - 109/123 controls were labeled correctly (88.6%)

The model is much better at identifying controls than impaired participants.

Accuracy: How Often Correct?

How often does the model get the class right?

\[ Accuracy = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN} \]

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  .metric  .estimator .estimate
  <chr>    <chr>          <dbl>
1 accuracy binary         0.802

Accuracy = 0.802 (80.2% classified correctly)

The Problem with Accuracy

Accuracy is easy to understand but has an important limitation.

It does not tell us which class the model gets wrong.

It can be misleading when classes are unbalanced.

Example: If 95% are controls, a model that always predicts “control” has 95% accuracy, despite failing to identify any impaired participants.

Specificity: Avoiding False Positives

Among people who are not “impaired”, how many does the model correctly identify?

Specificity measures how well the model identifies the negative class (controls).

\[ Sensitivity = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \]

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  .metric     .estimator .estimate
  <chr>       <chr>          <dbl>
1 specificity binary         0.886

Specificity = 0.886 (88.6% of controls correctly identified)

A highly specific model produces few false positives: it rarely labels a control as impaired.

Particularly useful when false positives are costly (e.g., unnecessary treatment, concern).

Sensitivity: Avoiding False Negatives

Among people who are “impaired”, how many does the model correctly identify?

Sensitivity measures how well the model identifies the positive class (impaired).

\[ Specificity = \frac{TN}{TN + FP} \]

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  .metric     .estimator .estimate
  <chr>       <chr>          <dbl>
1 sensitivity binary         0.568

Sensitivity = 0.568 (56.8% of impaired correctly identified)

A highly sensitive model produces few false negatives: it rarely misses an impaired participant.

Our model has high specificity (good at recognizing controls) but lower sensitivity (misses substantial proportion of impaired).

This distinction is crucial for understanding model performance.

Sensitivity vs Specificity

Specificity = 88.6%

  • Good at identifying controls
  • Few false positives
  • Conservative about calling impairment

Sensitivity = 56.8%

  • Misses many impaired cases
  • More false negatives
  • Not aggressive enough

Discussion Task

Discuss with your neighbor:

  • Which diagnosis would you prefer a lower probability threshold? Why?
  • Which diagnosis would you prefer a higher probability threshold? Why?

Consider consequences: - Cost of treatment - Side-effects - Effectiveness of treatment

Sensitivity and specificity depend on the chosen probability threshold.

Lower threshold: more willing to classify as impaired → higher sensitivity, lower specificity Higher threshold: more conservative → higher specificity, lower sensitivity

The “right” threshold depends on the costs of false positives vs false negatives.

Discrimination

ROC and AUC

Instead of choosing one threshold, we can look at model discrimination across all possible thresholds.

The ROC curve shows sensitivity against 1 − specificity.

ROC curve for cognitive impairment prediction

Area Under the Curve

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  .metric .estimator .estimate
  <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
1 roc_auc binary         0.840

AUC = area under the ROC curve

AUC can be interpreted as the probability that the model assigns a higher predicted probability to a randomly chosen “impaired” observation than to a randomly chosen “control” observation.

AUC measures discrimination (how well the model distinguishes between classes). It does NOT tell us whether the predicted probabilities themselves are accurate.

Calibration

Are the Probabilities Accurate?

Calibration asks a different question:

When the model says 70%, does the event happen about 70% of the time?

A simple calibration plot compares predicted probability with the observed proportion.

Calibration Plot

Calibration plot with breaks

A well-calibrated model follows the diagonal line.

Smooth Calibration Curve

Smooth calibration curve

Calibration is about the accuracy of the probabilities, not just the rankings.

A model can have excellent discrimination (high AUC) and poor calibration (probabilities don’t match observed frequencies).

The calibration model can be written as a logistic regression of the outcome on the logit of the predicted probability.

ABCD Framework in Detail

A: Calibration-in-the-large

Are predictions systematically too high or too low?

B: Calibration Slope

Are predictions too extreme or not extreme enough?

C: C-statistic

How well does the model discriminate between outcomes? (AUC)

D: Decision Curve

Does using the model improve clinical decisions?

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  term        estimate std.error statistic     p.value
  <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>       <dbl>
1 (Intercept)   -0.402     0.214     -1.88 0.0603     
2 logit_p        0.639     0.124      5.17 0.000000231

The intercept is related to calibration-in-the-large (A) and the coefficient of logit_p is the calibration slope (B).

Ideally: calibration-in-the-large ≈ 0 and calibration slope ≈ 1.

This is called the C-statistic of the AUC.

Prediction vs Effect Estimation

Different Questions

Prediction

How accurately can we predict what will happen?

  • Focus: accuracy of predictions
  • Tools: accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, AUC, calibration

Effect Estimation

How does changing a variable relate to what happens?

  • Focus: causal associations
  • Tools: regression coefficients, odds ratios

Important distinction:

A model can be excellent for prediction without giving an unbiased estimate of a causal effect.

The dataset ad_validation_logistic contains only predictions, not the original predictors, so we cannot recover the original regression coefficients.

What we can estimate is the association between the model’s predicted risk and the observed outcome (the calibration slope is one such measure).

Key Idea

No single metric evaluates a prediction model completely.

A useful model should: - Discriminate well - Produce sensible probabilities - Lead to better decisions

Summary: Evaluation Toolkit

Question Measure
Does the model classify correctly at this threshold? Accuracy
Does it avoid false positives? Specificity
Does it avoid false negatives? Sensitivity
Can it distinguish the two outcomes? ROC / AUC
Are the probabilities accurate? Calibration
Does it improve clinical decisions? Decision curve
What is the effect of a predictor? Effect estimate

The key idea: No single metric tells the whole story.

A useful model discriminates well, produces accurate probabilities, and improves decisions.
